title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Godzilla and King Ghidorah Battle to the Death in the Even Grander Follow-Up to ‘Godzilla Minus One’
description: Of all the criticisms leveled at Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” (apart from the one I have: that the entire movie is a frigging mess), the most r
body:
Of all the criticisms leveled at Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” (apart from the one I have: that the entire movie is a frigging mess), the most resonant, to me, was the complaint that Nolan had made a mistake by leaving the Greek gods out of the story. He certainly demonstrated that you could make a version of Homer minus the gods; he didn’t necessarily show that it could be done without losing a crucial dimension. Besides, if you can’t see gods at a movie of “The Odyssey,” where are you going to see them?
	

	The answer is: at a Japanese monster movie — more thrilling, by leagues, than “The Odyssey” — where the monsters possess an ominous majesty that’s not of this world, even as they’re in the middle of laying waste to it.


	In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which premiered tonight at the New York Film Festival (it opens Nov. 6), there are two oversize mystic beasts: Godzilla, the original kaiju (the character is now 72 years old, proving that 72 is the new awesome), and King Ghidorah, the dragon hydra who made his first appearance in the 1964 kaiju classic “Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster.” Each is a formidable creature, though in both cases it’s more than a matter of epic stomp or gargantuan wing power. When Godzilla tilts his head up to the sky, gathers his might, and then shoots out a blast of radioactivity that can level a city, it’s an exhibition of transcendent force. And Ghidorah’s heads — which look, up close, like costume figures out of a Golden Dragon Dance — emit orange lightning volts that extend for half a mile. These aren’t mere monsters. They’re serious movie gods.
	

	“Godzilla Minus Zero” is set in 1949, and it opens with a startling sequence in which Ghidorah, with only one head (this will change), shows up in the city of Matsumoto and destroys it. We’re given a grand vista of demolition, and also close-ups of Ghidorah seen from the point-of-view of Professor Murakami (Min Tanaka), a Hiroshima survivor who’s been doing biological creature research. Godzilla will soon turn up as well, even though he was thought to have been destroyed at the end of “Godzilla Minus One.” (It’s hard to destroy a god.) To save Japan, Kenji Noda (Hidetake Yoshioka), the high-strung, pencil-necked, Einstein-haired director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, leads his team in devising a plan that’s got a sandbox-showdown ingenuity: They will lure both creatures to a single locale and goad them into fighting each other. Whichever one remains standing will be wounded and weakened, and the human forces can then finish that monster off.

	When you go to see a big visual-effects movie, like something from Marvel, the closing credits that roll on for 12 minutes will feature multiple armies of visual-effects teams (each digital company with its own general). I have no doubt that a formidable army worked on “Godzilla Minus Zero.” But it’s also a movie that features the highly unusual credit “VFX, written, and directed by Takashi Yamazaki.” That’s a sign of how much the movie’s visual effects emanate directly from the imagination of the filmmaker. He’s writing, he’s directing, and he’s orchestrating spectacular gargantuan action paintings of beasts in motion. He’s an artist of larger-than-life pop horror.

	We’ve seen countless monster duels in kaiju movies (old and new, good and bad, Japanese and American), but Yamazaki, who rebooted the genre and took it to a new peak in the revelatory 2023 retro kaiju classic “Godzilla Minus One,” works with a quality that none of the filmmakers of recent decades has summoned: a fairy-tale innocence, an immersion in the annihilating heavy-metal poetry of Godzilla — the way the destruction of a city can become a spectacle out of a dream (which is to say, a national nightmare). In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” when Godzilla and King Ghidorah go at it, it’s more than a WWE match of primeval rivals. It’s a clash of the titans that will reduce everyone in the audience to a wide-eyed, jaw-dropped child.
	

	“Godzilla Minus One” was justly celebrated for its human story, which felt like something out of a Kurosawa movie of the ’50s. In “Godzilla Minus Zero,” Yamazaki follows through on that, continuing the tale of Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), the former World War II kamikaze pilot; Noriko (Minamo Hamabe), who is now his wife; and Akiko (Sae Nagatani), their adopted daughter, who has grown into a verbally precocious seven-year-old. The fate of this family is at the heart of the film’s emotional palette. To battle the creatures, Kōichi will go back into fighter-pilot mode, but the services of Noriko will be called on as well. She’s one of the survivors of Godzilla’s 1947 attack who now has bits of Godzilla DNA embedded in her body (which is why she wears an eyepatch).

	For a long time, kaiju movies were a semi-joke — a fusion of the colossal and the cheesy, and the fact that you couldn’t separate the two was part of what gave the genre its unique shlock magic. But Yamazaki transcends all that. His staging draws on our collective nostalgic memory of kaiju grandeur, and it also dignifies the genre by building it on a drama that’s staged with passion and vigor. When did anyone ever talk about performances in a Godzilla movie? But in “Godzilla Minus Zero,” one responds to the high anxiety of Yoshioka’s Noda, and to the magnetic intelligence of Masami Nagasawa as Makoto Aoyama, a meteorologist whose intuition about storms has a hint of the prophetic. Min Tanaka, who plays the professor, is an actor who was born on March 10, 1945, the day of the firebombing of Tokyo (the deadliest air raid in human history), and his courtly but simmering presence powerfully channels the film’s awareness of history. Yamazaki stages a couple of audacious sequences that feel, in their way, like his answer to “Oppenheimer.” One is a fantasy of Godzilla approaching Manhattan the way he once approached Tokyo, a chilling vision for any American to behold.

	At first, when the Japanese officials think that they’re contending only with Ghidorah, the film’s battles have a tactical stateliness. Ghidorah heads off to the mountains and hibernates, curling up like a giant snake, which makes them think they can bomb him into oblivion, using planes and weapons borrowed from the U.S. But all that accomplishes is to wake the sleeping giant. The sequence in which a half dozen planes battle Ghidorah in the air is grand, eye-popping filmmaking. And that’s just the appetizer, as Godzilla’s return heralds a battle of staggering vastness.
	

	In the final section, a plot strand or two gets a bit tangled. The professor has a hidden agenda, and how he ever meant to carry it out remains too abstract to be entirely clear. Yet as key characters are put under fire, we realize how much we’ve come to care about these creature battlers. They’re rooted in a time and place that feels all too real, and this allows the monsters to parade their primitive might in a way that means something. It was a stroke of inspiration on Yamazaki’s part to reset the kaiju genre in the late ’40s, during the Atomic Age where it is spiritually rooted (the original “Gojira” was released in 1954). The creators of the new James Bond series would do well to follow suit. (That’s how Bond could be vital again.) “Godzilla Minus Zero” is destined to connect with a huge international audience, and it’s already clear that this won’t be the last of Yamazaki’s kaiju epics. That’s because the movie proves that when you do it right, what seemed old can become timeless.

schema.headline: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Godzilla and King Ghidorah Battle to the Death in the Even Grander Follow-Up to ‘Godzilla Minus One’

title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Champions Franchise’s First R Rating as Sequel Rocks NYFF at World Premiere: ‘Censoring’ the Action ‘Was Not an Option’
description: “Godzilla Minus Zero” blew the roof off Alice Tully Hall during its rapturous world premiere screening at the New York Film Festival. The long-await
body:
“Godzilla Minus Zero” blew the roof off Alice Tully Hall during its rapturous world premiere screening at the New York Film Festival. The long-awaited sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” earned rave first reactions from the press earlier in the day, and that adoration rolled right into the world premiere. The movie was met with multiple mid-screening applauses as the crowd went wild for all the kaiju mayhem on screen.

	Ahead of its debut later this year, “Godzilla Minus Zero” has been rated R for “violent content/bloody images,” making it the first entry in the 72-year-old franchise to receive an R-rating. Director Takashi Yamazaki, returning to helm the sequel after 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” became a roaring success, says securing the rating was “essential to the film.”“Logically, as a studio — and even as a director — you want as many people from the general public to be able to see your film,” Yamazaki told Variety at the premiere Saturday afternoon. “So, an R-rating might seem like a barrier to entry, and conversations about, ‘Hey, could we have not gotten this down to PG-13?’ of course are going to happen. In spite of that, though, there were certain scenes that, for me as a director, were so essential to the film. Censoring it or cutting it was just not an option for me.”
	

	Under MPA guidelines, viewers under 17 cannot attend an R-rated film without a parent or guardian, a restriction that has traditionally made the rating a commercial deterrent for studios releasing big-budget, four-quadrant films. That stigma has faded over the past decade, starting with the blockbuster success of 2016’s “Deadpool” ($782 million). In 2019, “Joker” ($1.07 billion) became the first R-rated film to cross the $1 billion threshold. That record was later broken by 2024’s “Deadpool & Wolverine” ($1.33 billion) — and more recently — 2026’s “The Odyssey” ($1.72 billion), which currently stands as the 17th highest-grossing film of all time worldwide.


	“I think the R-rating, at one point, carried almost a negative connotation,” Yamazaki explained. “In more modern films, it actually creates a sort of expectation and excitement of, ‘Okay, well, they’re not censoring anything. The director and the cast’s voice is there, as is.’ So it is very encouraging to see other films who have preceded us that have already found a lot of success with the R-rating at the box office. Hopefully, we can continue that trend with ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.’”
	

	Inside the world premiere screening, New York Film Festival director Dennis Lim acknowledged that the Godzilla franchise might not be the first thing people think of playing at a major film festival. And yet, “We thought it was about time to bring a giant monster movie here.”

	Yamazaki took the stage to thunderous applause from the audience both before and after the screening, where he asked the crowd not to spoil any of the sequel’s many surprises on social media.

	“You are the first to see this film,” the filmmaker said. “There are a lot of ‘Godzilla’ fans around the world, so let’s work together and do not do any spoilers. No spoilers, please! I am trusting all of you guys.”

	Yamazaki also had the audience laughing while explaining how he never intended to create a sequel to “Godzilla Minus One.” Executives at Toho immediately started asking him about a follow-up movie once they saw the first cut of “Minus One,” a thought that made Yamazaki instantly nervous. It wasn’t until the movie opened in theaters and started to be celebrated around the world by audiences that the director realized a sequel would be a viable option.

	“Toho executives are here now,” the director said. “Hopefully all your reactions tonight don’t have them wanting a third movie.”

schema.headline: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Champions Franchise’s First R Rating as Sequel Rocks NYFF at World Premiere: ‘Censoring’ the Action ‘Was Not an Option’

title: Jon Watts to Direct Next ‘Star Wars’ Movie
description:
A new “Star Wars” movie is currently in development with director Jon Watts attached.

	Watts is best known for directing the popular “Spider-Man” t
body:
A new “Star Wars” movie is currently in development with director Jon Watts attached.

	Watts is best known for directing the popular “Spider-Man” trilogy starring Tom Holland, which includes 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming,” 2019’s “Spider-Man: Far From Home,” and 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home.” (2026’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was directed by Destin Daniel Cretton.) Before being selected to direct “Spider-Man,” Watts also helmed films including “Cop Car” and “Clown.” Following his involvement with the trilogy, In 2024, it was reported that Watts, his production company Freshman Year and producer Dianne McGunigle had signed a first-look feature deal with Walt Disney Studios.
	

	In 2024, Watts co-created “Skeleton Crew” alongside Christopher Ford, a coming-of-age series set in the era of the New Republic that followed four young characters on a new adventure, per the show’s official logline. Jude Law starred as Jod Na Nawood, with Ravi Cabot-Conyers as Wim, Ryan Kiera Armstrong as Fern, Kyriana Kratter as KB and Robert Timothy Smith as Neel.


	With the role, Watts joins a list of previous “Star Wars” directors that includes Irvin Kershner, Richard Marquand, J.J. Abrams, Rian Johnson and “Star Wars” creator George Lucas. Released in 2019, Abrams’ “Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker” is the most recent film in the franchise to debut theatrically.

	As previously reported by Variety, Simon Kinberg will pen the script for the film. Kinberg is best known for being a writer, producer and director for the “X-Men” franchise, and was considered a surprising choice at the time of the announcement.
	

	Knight Edge Media first broke the news.

schema.headline: Jon Watts to Direct Next ‘Star Wars’ Movie

title: Robert Pattinson Says It Would Be ‘Tough’ for His Batman to Exist Within James Gunn’s DCU
description: Superman and Batman might be one of the DC Universe’s most famous partnerships, but Robert Pattinson is officially ending speculation that his take
body:
Superman and Batman might be one of the DC Universe’s most famous partnerships, but Robert Pattinson is officially ending speculation that his take on Bruce Wayne would fit in the cinematic world created by James Gunn.

	“I think it would be kind of tough to have this version of Bruce outside of that world,” Pattinson told LADbible. “It’s one of the only characters, I guess, because of the length of the shoots, but also it’s such a specific kind of [style]; the tone of it gets inside you. I remember that happened to me the last time I did it, it took a while. You’re just in the dark the whole time. Both mood-wise and light-wise, I can’t see anything for like months. It does affect you, like you feel strange afterwards.”
	

	Audiences were first introduced to Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” in 2022, which offered a distinctly darker take on the comic book character than previous films. “Where do you go after ‘The Dark Knight’? Ben Affleck blew it, and even Christopher Nolan, who brought unprecedented levels of realism and gravitas to that franchise-best Batman saga, couldn’t improve on what he’d created in his 2012 sequel,” wrote Variety’s Peter Debruge in his review of the film. “So what is ‘Cloverfield’ director Matt Reeves’ strategy? Answer: Go darker than ‘The Dark Knight,’ deadlier than ‘No Time to Die’ and longer than ‘Dune’ with a serious-minded Batman stand-alone of his own.”


	By contrast, Gunn’s “Superman,” released in 2025, was a lighter take on the character. Variety’s Owen Gleiberman wrote that “the new movie isn’t ‘dark’ (Zack Snyder’s ambitious mistake) so much as it’s a loopy, spinning, multifaceted story with genuine emotional stakes.”
	

	“The Batman Part II” is set to hit theaters on Feb. 18, 2028.

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson Says It Would Be ‘Tough’ for His Batman to Exist Within James Gunn’s DCU

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Mocks Donald Trump and Andy Burnham’s First Meeting, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and More in Wild Weekend Update
description:
U.S. President Donald Trump, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and more were mocked in the latest “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Weekend Update segment.

	“T
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and more were mocked in the latest “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Weekend Update segment.

	“This week, President Trump welcomed President Xi to the White House,” co-anchor Ania Magliano said. “As a sign of respect, Trump wore a bright red tie as a sign of Communist China. And Xi wore a mottled purple tie, the color of Trump’s prostate.”


	Joking about Trump’s Chinese banquet for President Xi, Magliano quipped: “Trump ordered a 20, an 18 and a 21. And afterwards sat down for a Chinese-inspired banquet.”
	

	“From Beijing to beige man, Trump met [U.K. Prime Minister] Andy Burnham” Young continued. “It wasn’t a memorable event for Trump, as he’s got dementia.”

	Altman, the co-founder of OpenAI, and his appearance at the UN was also teased. “Altman, whose company launched ChatGPT, warned his creation could destroy humanity. And then he slapped his own wrists and ran out of the room saying, ‘Someone stop me!’” Magliano said.

	“SNL U.K.” also took aim at Harvey Weinstein, who was sentenced to 15 years in prison in New York earlier this week.

	“Me Too is now what the inmates say in the queue for Weinstein’s arsehole,” Magliano joked as the audience let out a collective “oooh.”

	“Back in 2016, Weinstein hired a private intelligence firm to dig up dirt on his victims,” Young continued. “So on one side, we have a prolific rapist with paid spies. On the other, we have abuse victims who have been silenced. A conflict described by Ed Sheeran as ‘nuanced.’”
	

	Elsewhere, Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu’s recent speech at the UN — where representatives for other nations walked out — was also mentioned. “Of course, it is easy to paint Netanyahu as the bad guy in this situation,” Young said before swiftly moving on to the next item.

schema.headline: ‘SNL U.K.’ Mocks Donald Trump and Andy Burnham’s First Meeting, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and More in Wild Weekend Update

title: ‘Jack & Christine’ Trailer: John Hawkes Turns A Dinner Party Into A Night of Chaos – Film News in Brief
description:
“Jack & Christine,” a thriller short film starring John Hawkes, released the first trailer ahead of its world premiere at Beyond Fest on Sunday.

	T
body:
“Jack & Christine,” a thriller short film starring John Hawkes, released the first trailer ahead of its world premiere at Beyond Fest on Sunday.

	The trailer shows married couple Jack (Luke Barnett) and Christine (Nikki Lorenzo) hosting a dinner party that suddenly spirals into an intense, chaotic evening when a guest (Hawkes) from the couple’s past arrives.

	“I’ve always been fascinated by anxiety and paranoia, especially when they start to manifest as reality,” said Noam Kroll, the film’s writer and director. “The theme of this film can be summed up in a line from Catch-22: ‘Just because you’re paranoid doesn’t mean they aren’t after you.’ The idea had been in my head for years, and when I got the chance to work with these three incredible actors, I wrote a chamber piece tailored to each of them.”
	

	“Jack & Christine” is produced by Kroll, Richard Handley, Sheldon Brigman, Jennifer Kroll and Dave Thies. Watch the trailer below.




	Michael B. Jordan Joins CultureCon 2026 Lineup

	This year’s CultureCon lineup will feature reigning best actor Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan. 

	Following the blockbuster and commercial success of “Sinners,” Jordan is preparing to release his second directorial effort, “The Thomas Crown Affair,” and he’s gearing up to shoot the upcoming “Miami Vice” reboot.

	“Lanterns” star Aaron Pierre and musicians Wale and Tobe Nwigwe are also joining the lineup for the 2026 edition of the annual festival, designed to celebrate and empower the next generation of creators of color.
	

	This year’s CultureCon, held October 3-4 in Brooklyn, is backed by presenting sponsor Chase Ink and a host of other companies, including Cricket Wireless, Lincoln, HBO Max, Audible and TikTok. The two-day program will also feature appearances by Oscar winners John Legend, Mahershala Ali and Daniel Kaluuya; Emmy winner Niecy Nash-Betts; and culture shifters like Colin Kaepernick, Olandria Carthen, Miles Caton, Danessa Myricks, Rajah Caruth, Scott Evans and Sherri Shepherd. 

	Tickets are available on CultureCon’s website.
	
		Phil Lord, Chris Miller Named Guest Artistic Directors for AFI Fest 2026	

	“Project Hail Mary” filmmakers Phil Lord and Chris Miller were announced as the Guest Artistic Directors for AFI FEST 2026.

	This year’s program will include “An Evening with Lord and Miller,” which features a Q&A with the directors followed by a screening of “2001: A Space Odyssey,” held at the TCL Chinese Theatre on Oct. 24.

	The filmmakers have also curated a selection of films inspired by their work on “Project Hail Mary.” The slate includes “Harold and Maude” (1971), “The Muppet Movie” (1979) and “Rififi” (1955).

	“After years of dragging our friends and families to screenings of films we love, we are delighted to get to do it for hundreds of strangers,” Lord and Miller said in a joint statement. “We chose four films that inspired us not only while making ‘Project Hail Mary’ but also as filmmakers and people. We stand on the shoulders of giants like Hal Ashby and Fozzie Bear.”

	AFI FEST 2026 will run Oct. 21-25 at the TCL Chinese Theatre. The festival opens with the U.S. premiere of “Wildwood,” features the world premiere of “The Mosquito Bowl” and closes with “Being Heumann,” with the full lineup being announced Sept. 29.
	
		‘Club Kid’ Gets 35mm Pre-Release Screening at San Francisco’s Castro Theatre	

	SFFilm will present a special preview screening A24’s “Club Kid” in 35mm at San Francisco’s Castro Theatre on Nov. 2 at 7:00 p.m. with writer, director and star Jordan Firstman making an appearance for a post-screening conversation.

	“’Club Kid’ is an exhilarating introduction to Jordan Firstman as a filmmaker, with a world that feels completely specific and wonderfully alive,” SFFilm director of programming Jessie Fairbanks said. “The anarchic humor, incredible ensemble, and unexpected tenderness make this a distinctive film, elevated by needle drops that are thrillingly precise to the characters, culture, and emotional landscape of the story. Bay Area audiences will be treated to a 35mm print, a rare and special way to experience a night at the movies.”
	

	The film follows “a hard-partying New York City club promoter sees his whirlwind lifestyle upended by the arrival of the 10-year-old son he never knew he had.”

	A24 opens “Club Kid” in limited release starting on Nov. 6.

	Anne Lai, SFFILM’s Executive Director, said, “One of the most exciting things we do at SFFILM is to introduce bold new filmmakers to eager and welcoming audiences. There is not a more fitting place than the iconic Castro Theatre to welcome Jordan Firstman with his feature directorial debut. For decades, gathering to see movies at The Castro has been at the heart of San Francisco’s queer culture and history. We can’t wait to share ‘Club Kid’ at this cinema sanctuary for what’s sure to become one for the ages.”
	
		“The Debut” and “Paper Tiger” Among 2026 Virginia Film Festival Lineup, Jessica Lange and Nathan Lane to Receive Visionary Awards	

	The Virginia Film Festival announced the lineup for its 39th year, which will take place Oct. 21-25. 

	Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” starring Julianne Moore, will open the festival, while “1 15 41 Tragedy to Triumph” serves as the closing night film. The Centerpiece Film is “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” starring Amanda Seyfried, and writer, director, producer and actor Tim Blake Nelson will receive the festival’s Virtuoso Award. 

	In addition to appearing as keynote guests, Nathan Lane and Jessica Lange will receive Visionary Awards, and James Gray will be awarded with the Outstanding Achievement in Directing Award at a screening of “Paper Tiger.” Also screening at the festival are “14th,” “Club Kid,” “I Play Rocky,” “Ink,” “Wild Horse Nine” and “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York.” 

	The full program will be available on the Virginia Film Festival website on Thursday.

schema.headline: ‘Jack & Christine’ Trailer: John Hawkes Turns A Dinner Party Into A Night of Chaos – Film News in Brief

title: Emmy Rossum Says Nude ‘Shameless’ Scenes Affected Her Dating Life Because Men Had ‘Preconceived Notions’ of ‘How I Was Sexually’
description:
Emmy Rossum recently revealed that playing Fiona Gallagher on “Shameless” had some lasting consequences off-screen.

	Rossum’s nude scenes in the sh
body:
Emmy Rossum recently revealed that playing Fiona Gallagher on “Shameless” had some lasting consequences off-screen.

	Rossum’s nude scenes in the show, which ran for nine seasons, made her dating life difficult because of “preconceived notions,” she said. “It got quite tricky because of the nudity on the show,” Rossum told Maria Sharapova on an episode of “Pretty Tough.” “All of the guys that I would go out with had preconceived notions of who I was or how I was sexually.”
	

	Some of the conversations were “bizarre,” Rossum said, noting one particular experience in which a man hoping to pursue a career in politics was hesitant about being associated with her because of the scenes. 


	“He was like, ‘I really want to be president someday.’ And I was like, ‘Wow, that’s a great goal,’” she said. “He’s like, ‘But I feel like running for office dating someone who’s been exposed in the way that you have — do you think that would be tricky for me?’ And I was like, ‘This is an insane conversation to have.’”

	Rossum began “Shameless” when she was just 24, which she said was a difficult time to attempt dating as a young actress.

	“You’re trying to figure out who you are,” she said. “You’re coming into your own as an artist. And there’s also all these preconceived notions about you that are out there that are associated with [you] because your body is your art, right? And people can get confused.”

	Prior to “Shameless,” Rossum starred in “The Day After Tomorrow,” “Mystic River” and “The Phantom of the Opera,” the latter of which earned her a Golden Globes nomination.

schema.headline: Emmy Rossum Says Nude ‘Shameless’ Scenes Affected Her Dating Life Because Men Had ‘Preconceived Notions’ of ‘How I Was Sexually’

title: ‘NAZA’ Co-Director Yuval Abraham Calls Out the U.S. Government for ‘Funding’ Israel’s Destruction of Gaza, Telling NYFF Audience: ‘This Is What Your Country Is Supporting’
description: The Gaza documentary “NAZA” made its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival to a massive standing ovation for co-directors Yuval Abra
body:
The Gaza documentary “NAZA” made its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival to a massive standing ovation for co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor who gave a brief Q&A with festival director Dennis Lim after the screening. Journalist and co-director Abraham told the crowd, many of whom were still drying their eyes after bearing witness in the documentary to footage of the destruction of Gaza, that it was essential to play “NAZA” at NYFF because the U.S. is responsible for funding billions to the Israeli government and supplying military aid, which is being used against the Palestinian people.
	

	“It’s important for us to see this film at this moment, as you were saying, because these older officials are talking about what is being done with taxpayer money from people sitting here,” said Abraham, who was met with cheers of approval from the audience. “This is what your country is supporting and funding… Part of the goal is to make denial of what’s going on in Gaza harder.” 


	“NAZA” first premiered at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, where it won a special jury prize and received a record-breaking 24.5-minute standing ovation. The documentary was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv and shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.” It is now set to release in more than 50 territories before becoming available to stream for free on The Guardian’s website.

	Since its premiere, the directors have come under fire from a number of Israeli officials — Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for the introduction of a law that would “revoke the citizenship of anyone who slanders IDF [Israeli Defense Forces] soldiers” following the film’s debut, while Israel’s Minister of Culture threatened to revoke the filmmaker’s Israeli citizenship. 
	

	Outside the festival screening, the Israeli-American Council organized a more than 50-person protest against the film, which they described as “anti-Israel,” and said “makes serious allegations about the IDF’s conduct in the Gaza Strip while ignoring findings and information that contradict its claims.” Those in attendance gathered by LED trucks that projected footage from October 7 and portraits of those who were killed that day. 

	“It’s completely unjustified, the massacre of October 7th,” said Abraham during the Q&A. “But it also cannot justify what you’ve seen. Does it justify the slaughter of so many civilians in Gaza?”

schema.headline: ‘NAZA’ Co-Director Yuval Abraham Calls Out the U.S. Government for ‘Funding’ Israel’s Destruction of Gaza, Telling NYFF Audience: ‘This Is What Your Country Is Supporting’

title: ‘My Sad Dead’ Review: An Urban Community Gets the Haunting It Deserves in Pablo Larraín’s Superb Modern Gothic
description: Macabre and melancholy but suffused with a delicious absurdism that somehow doesn’t clog the arteries of its hopeful little heart, Pablo Larraín‘s s
body:
Macabre and melancholy but suffused with a delicious absurdism that somehow doesn’t clog the arteries of its hopeful little heart, Pablo Larraín‘s sprawling, peculiar, terrific “My Sad Dead” is about 20 things at once in every moment. It’s a ghost story, obviously, on account of all the ghosts. It’s a droll tragicomedy, with eccentrically deadpan characters providing both the tragedy and the jokes. It’s a nasty body-horror and a ferocious satire — in its way as scathing a portrait of modern, urban Argentina as any of Larraín’s previous Chilean films have been about his homeland. And most surprisingly, it’s a mini-treatise on hostile urban architecture and the effect it has on the human spirit to dwell in brutal, brutalist structures that quarantine their inhabitants from society, and from each other. “Rage weighs more than concrete,” sings Shakira over the closing credits, but the Piedrabuena neighborhood of Buenos Aires is heavy with both.
	

	Ema (Mercedes Morán, in a fantastic performance of dry eyes and drier wit) is almost an emblem of Piedrabuena, though her rage has long since turned to a resilient kind of resignation, only tempered by the quick flash of amusement that often sparks up in her otherwise world-weary expression. Or should that be otherworld-weary? Ema doesn’t sleep much because of all the screaming ghosts who, for now, only she can hear. 


	A doctor who has been pushed into retirement, with dark mutterings going on about a trolley-problem decision she made regarding COVID treatments, Ema doesn’t technically live in Piedrabuena anymore — she has a spacious apartment in a nicer part of the city that she is looking to rent out. But she has recently moved back to care for her aged mother through the terminal stages of a painful illness. And that’s how we first see her, from above, as we hover like an angel or an overhead lamp, in the attic room of her mother’s house beside the Piedrabuena projects. Ema holds the bedridden woman’s frail, pale blue hand as, not particularly quietly nor entirely peacefully, she dies. Then her corpse opens its eyes.
	

	It’s not her, exactly, but a fuzzy, not-quite-opaque facsimile of her. The effect that “My Sad Dead” uses to summon the dead is the more convincing for not being particularly flashy. The unusual, low-contrast color palette that Larraín and his ace regular DP Sergio Armstrong have chosen blanches the images to a flat, pinkish gray, so that those with and without heartbeats all have the pallor of a mortuary waiting room’s magnolia walls. 

	Yet we always know who is alive and who is, well, post-alive, and not just because the dead often have a tell, like they’ll be staggering around with half their head blown off, or bleeding copiously from a ragged, ripped-open chest wound. It’s also because of their manner. Ema tends not to encounter too many quiet, dignified, expected deaths, and those who have experienced a violent end are almost childlike in their confusion and disorientation. Often they seem trapped in a cycle, doomed to re-live (and re-die) their last moments, powerless to change the outcome.

	Ema is sick of the dead and long past sick of trying to convince others that her abilities are real. So mostly she ignores the ghosts and they ignore her and that’s fine. But then her estranged sister Lidia (Alejandra Flechner) and her husband fly in for a visit from their home in Seattle, bringing with them their troubled, morbidly obese teenage daughter Julia (Carolina Álvarez), and Ema comes to realize that Julia can also commune with the dead. 

	And really commune: Julia, miserable and stigmatized and about to be committed to an institution by her hapless parents, loudly and lustily enjoys getting busy with the no-longer-with-us in a way that one supposes cannot technically be necrophilia, considering it’s sex with the spirits of the dead rather than with their bodies. Which doesn’t mean Larraín averts our gaze from these strangely moving copulations; the film is about the non-corporeal but it’s fascinated too by the flesh, by its gratification, its mortification and then, in an increasingly ethereal refrain, its slow putrefaction and decomposition.

	With its octagonal clusters of flats arranged around a central water tower that looks like a fist raised against the sky, the neighborhood doesn’t have much spirit of community. The residents occasionally gather in a disused rec center but the meetings devolve into rants about immigrants, junkies, thugs and vigilantism. One man suggests mounting the heads of thieves on spikes, a grisly image that Larraín, for once, spares us, as opposed to the bungling burglar falling from a roof and impaling himself crunchily on a railing, or the three pretty, giggling teens who get shot and shot and shot again in a gang-related hit, or the young woman who dies agonisingly of an infected dog bite she concealed because she couldn’t afford to miss work. 
	

	Ema cannot fix these restless ghosts, but sometimes she can distract them from the shock of their painful passing, a talent which puts her in demand when the water supply becomes mysteriously contaminated, and suddenly the whole of Piedrabuena can hear what she has always heard. The screams, the gunshots and the cries for help that went unanswered.

	In other hands, this would set up a supernatural TV procedural. But Ema does not solve mysteries or bring murderers to justice. “My Sad Dead” has no interest in being “Medium” and its provenance as TV — it was conceived as a Netflix miniseries but recut into this 186-minute movie for a San Sebastián competition bow — only proves that cinematic storytelling has little to do with the size of the screen on which you watch it. It is entirely cinematic, every scene loaded with texture and subtext and observational nuance. If there’s a comparison, it may be with Krzysztof Kieślowski’s “Dekalog,” also nominally a television project and also one set within a single housing complex. (It feels like we’ve been talking about “Dekalog” a lot recently, given the ongoing project to remake it. Perhaps there’s something in the water.) 

	But really, the similarity is in mood and effect. Larraín, alongside Anastasia Ayazi and Guillermo Calderón, co-scripts with Mariana Enriquez, whose writings provide the foundational inspiration, and their outstanding screenplay tells a hundred little side-stories in addition to its main narrative. Almost all of them are harsh or gross or scary or sorrowful and yet the experience of “My Sad Dead” is mordantly funny and oddly uplifting. Maybe it’s the weirdness. Maybe it’s the way it makes a waterlogged ribbon of skin detaching from a shin and floating away seem deeply beautiful. Or maybe it’s just a reminder that being sad about death — your own or someone else’s — is simply an upside-down affirmation that you are happy to be alive.

schema.headline: ‘My Sad Dead’ Review: An Urban Community Gets the Haunting It Deserves in Pablo Larraín’s Superb Modern Gothic

title: ‘The Simpsons’ Boss on Season Premiere Guests Emma Thompson and Colin Jost; ‘Treehouse of Horror’ Spoilers; Jack in the Box Meal Easter Eggs and Movie Update
description: “The Simpsons” returns on Sunday, Sept. 27, on Fox with a Season 38 opener (“The Children’s Book Job”) that parodies children’s books, featuring gue
body:
“The Simpsons” returns on Sunday, Sept. 27, on Fox with a Season 38 opener (“The Children’s Book Job”) that parodies children’s books, featuring guest voice Emma Thompson as a beloved children’s book author who comes to town for a benefit to save Springfield Elementary from closing.

	But when her character — saucy British writer Constance Clavinger — turns out to be a handful (getting drunk at the airport bar, for starters), Homer struggles to get her to the school on time. They go on an adventure across town as he tries to get her, “Get Him to the Greek” style, to a school book fair organized by new PTA president Marge. 
	



	

	



	Colin Jost also appears as himself, reading his own children’s book to the Springfield Elementary audience, much to their indifference.


	In one sequence, Homer daydreams that Springfield and its citizens have turned into settings and characters from kids’ books like “The Very Hungry Caterpillar,” Richard Scarry’s universe, “Don’t Let the Pigeon Drive the Bus,” “Captain Underpants,” “Diary of a Wimpy Kid” and more.

	“The genesis of this was, when you’re lucky enough to work on ‘The Simpsons,’ you can ask yourself, ‘What kind of cool thing can we portray in the Matt Groening/‘Simpsons’ style that we’ve never done?’” says executive producer Matt Selman. “And one of those are classic children’s books, like ‘Make Way for Ducklings.’”

	Selman calls the episode a “love letter” to that world of children’s books. “I love my love letters,” he says. “Richard Scarry, Eric Carle from ‘The Hungry Caterpillar,’ all these generational children’s artists. We got really excited about that.”
	

	Dan Vebber is the credited writer on the episode, while Matthew Nastuk is the director; Selman says Vebber and co-executive producer Mike Price cooked up the story idea, “a take on the ‘mild-mannered person has to get crazy person from ‘Point A’ to Point B’ kind of story … Two people thrown together in crazy situations become friends, become enemies and then become friends again. I love a good ’80s movie structure. So, for all the people who still love ‘Get Him to the Greek,’ this is the episode for you!”

	Thompson’s character plays a large role in the episode. “If you’re going to write a giant guest part, you want an icon, a bucket list person like Emma Thompson,” Selman says. “And she threw herself into it with full gusto. It’s sort of an interesting season premiere in that you’re meeting a new character and it’s kind of Homer’s side adventure.”

	Homer is enlisted to pick up Constance — and, realizing that he has been spending too much time ignoring his family and playing a free game on his phone, ultimately decides to make up for it by saving the day.

	“It makes a lot of great points about parenting and trying not to be a checked-out parent,” Selman says. “And this line I like in it, Homer says, ‘children’s books are a better parent than I’ll ever be.’ It’s a good little bit of truthfulness there from Homer.”



	

	



	Among more upcoming episodes, “Diary of a Chimpy Kid” (Oct. 4) follows Bart and Lisa as they adopt a baby chimp. “Homer watches a YouTube video about what adult chimps do to their human owners, which is bite off their fingers, faces and genitals,” Selman says. “And Homer becomes terrified of a baby chimp as Bart and Lisa learn how to co-parent. There’s some genital mutilation comedy in that one, but I am very pleased with it!”

	In another upcoming episode, “The Kosmic Kruiser,” Bart and Lisa are trapped in an abandoned immersive theme park experience. And “Testing 1-2-3” will look at the world of neurodiversity. “I think it’s terrific,” Selman says of threading the needle on that one between being funny and being empathetic. “We’re very proud of it.”

	As for “Treehouse of Horror XXXVII” (Oct. 25), the original opening is a “Simpsons”/“Nightmare Before Christmas” mashup, produced by Stoopid Buddy Stoodios — featuring “Simpsons” versions of the “Nightmare Before Christmas” characters.
	

	Then, one segment is inspired by the British novel “The Husbands,” by Holly Gramazio, in which Homer goes to the shed and comes out as a different husband for Marge. Suddenly, she’s married to Lenny. Or Kang and Kodos. Tiffany Haddish guests as Marge’s best friend in one of her new husband realities, “kind of like how in rom-coms characters always have a sassy best friend,” Selman notes. “She lectures Marge about dating, and it’s like a stand-up set.”

	Another segment is described as “Freaky Friday” meets “Pet Sematary,” where “Homer accidentally kills Bart and the dog and buries them, and they come back just having their bodies switched. And in the third one, “Homer mysteriously vanished years ago, and the teenage versions of Bart and Lisa find out that evil witch versions of Patty and Selma have trapped him in endless murderous Driver’s Ed films.”

	This year’s “Treehouse of Horror” is timed to the show’s current tie-in with Jack in the Box. The fast-food chain is currently promoting a “Munchie Meal of Horror,” featuring six collectable glow-in the dark cups (which have already sold out at many locations).

	“One of the great joys of this job is to do these little collabs with industries you’re not part of, like fast food or video games or toys or theme parks or whatever,” Selman says. “These collectible cups are just gorgeous and pretty high quality. Like everything we do, they sold out in one second. Yeah. Now they’re on eBay for $200. I said, ‘make sure you make enough cups!’ And they said, ‘we know about how many cups to make.’ And guess what? They didn’t!”



	

	



	The “Simpsons” meals are full of references from the show — like Bart’s twin brother Hugo, from Season 8, who appears on a cup. “In that episode, Hugo would eat fish heads, and in our version of the cup, Hugo is eating the Jack in the Box fish sandwich. It’s just very fun to do a 30-year fish callback.”

	Selman admits that “I procrastinated from working on the stuff that I should be working on by working really hard on this box. And there are so many ‘Simpsons’ Easter eggs on this box that you would think it was Easter, not Halloween. You can quote me on that. Definitely quote me on that.”

	And here’s perhaps the ultimate obscure Easter egg: On the “Munchie Meal of Horror” box, several “Simpsons” characters are dressed like the now-obscure 1970s era “Jack in the Box Bunch” like the “Hamburgermeister,” “Onion Ring Thing” and “Secret Sauce Agent.” (Those characters were eliminated in 1980, but a grown-up version of “Jack” returned in 1994 — this time in a suit and round clown head. He’s still the chain’s spokesperson today.
	

	“When I was a kid, I would go to Jack in the Box, and there was the Jack in the Box version of the McDonaldland gang that no one remembers but me. It was a very goofy bunch of fast food mascots. And so I made the bullies wear those costumes. That’s what the bullies are dressed up as, and people are like, ‘Who are they dressed as?’ They’re dressed as the 1970s Jack in the Box Gang: Secret Sauce Agent, Onion Ring Thing and Hamburgermeister. I haven’t gone on the internet to see if anyone has figured this out! But that is a big mashup.”

	The meal box also includes comical gravestones with dead “Simpsons” favorites like Frank Grimes. “I bet he didn’t think he’d ever be on a Munchie Meal box, right?” Selman says.

	He adds: “This is how hard the movie is that I’m just throwing myself into these boxes.”

	Oh yes, the movie. How’s that going? The new “Simpsons” movie is currently slated to premiere on Sept. 3, 2027 (shifted from its original July 23 date). It’s already written, and yes, it may have a title. But Selman won’t share just yet.

	“The working title is ‘New Simpsons Movie,’ but we might have an actual title,” he says. “It hasn’t been approved yet. But [the movie] is going to be great! It’s already ’S’ tier.”

	S tier? “People love to rank things on the internet as part of our reductive society that we live in, right? People will rank things between F-D-C-B-A, and then S is the best. And people will do it for everything. What’s the best protein drink? What’s the best Alan Moore graphic novel? So, the movie’s going to be S tier. That’s my promise to you.”

	Here’s the logline to “The Simpsons” Season 38 premiere, “The Children’s Book Job”: “Marge hopes to save Springfield Elementary by inviting a reclusive British children’s author (guest star Emma Thompson) to appear at the school’s book fair. But Homer botches his assignment of picking the author up at the airport, and the drunken pepper pot leads him on a desperate wild chase to get her to the school on time.” The episode airs Sunday, Sept. 27, at 8 p.m. on Fox, and streams the next day on Hulu. 

	Here’s an exclusive first look at Emma Thompson in the premiere episode:

title: Johnny Depp Bites Into a Decorative Plant at Vegas Event
description:
Johnny Depp
                          I'm Literally Chewing the Scenery!!!
body:
Johnny Depp
                          I'm Literally Chewing the Scenery!!!
                      
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Johnny Depp is known for never blending into the background ... but at a recent Vegas event, he literally started eating it.
      
    
            While attending Drink Las Vegas -- a four-day event across multiple hotels -- at Park MGM last night, the "Pirates of the Caribbean" actor stopped to pose for photos ... and, well ... munch on some plants.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In the video obtained by TMZ ... Johnny bit a leaf from the photo call's backdrop before chewing on it in front of the event's attendees.
      

            After spitting out the green ... the Oscar-nominated actor went back for round 2 and chomped on an even bigger piece of the step-and-repeat wall.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Johnny seemed to be in good spirits ... so it looks like he was just having a bit of fun with a few photographers!
      
    
            Well, Johnny has a lot to be happy about ... the lawsuit against his band, Hollywood Vampires, was dismissed by a judge.

title: Sylvester Stallone Opens Up About Severe Anxiety & Recurring Attacks
description:
Sylvester Stallone
                          My First Anxiety-Induced Attack Nearly KO'd Me!
body:
Sylvester Stallone
                          My First Anxiety-Induced Attack Nearly KO'd Me!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                September 26, 2026
                
                            12:44 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 26, 2026
                                3:07 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sylvester Stallone is opening up about how he's quietly suffered anxiety-induced attacks for decades ... and how his diagnosis still plays a part in his life.
      
    
            In a wide-ranging, candid interview with The New York Times, Sylvester said the first time he suffered from an anxiety-induced attack was when he was watching daily footage from a film project in his mid-30s.
      
    
            He said ... "The first time was when I was 36 and I was watching dailies, and then all of a sudden I stood up and the hair on my neck went up and I started getting hot and I go, I’m dying, this is it, I’m on my way out. And bang, down I went. Took a knee, crawled, rolled over, and now I’m in this dark movie theater."
      
    
            While Sylvester didn't label the episodes as panic attacks ... he did say he suffered similar moments of crippling anxiety "again and again and again."
      
    
            The "Rocky" star said that the attacks come out of nowhere ... and are something he still deals with as he gets older.
      
    
            He said ... "When I’m in a crowd, I’d be with my wife at an art exhibition and the room is filling up. It’s getting more and more, and then I’d go, 'I'm going down,' and she’d be like, 'Let’s get out of here.' And literally I just make it to the alley, boom, get down on one knee."
